strengths: First asymptotic analysis of attention in the extensive-rank regime; derives sharp learning curves, thresholds, and spectral laws with exact asymptotics
Exceptional quantitative agreement between theoretical predictions and Adam simulations (Figures 1-3) across broad range of sample complexities despite non-convexity
Rigorously formalizes how weight decay induces nuclear-norm regularization on attention matrices, clarifying implicit bias toward low-rank solutions
Cleanly isolates inductive bias of factorized vs. non-factorized parameterization through theoretical comparison and experiments
Reproduces key empirical phenomena observed in transformers: low-rank structure, separated spectral outliers as samples increase
Methodologically solid: extends AMP theory to multi-token softmax setting with non-separable priors; combines GMT and AMP in novel way
Excellent reproducibility: code provided, extensive appendices with detailed derivations, computational implementation details specified
Honestly acknowledges model simplifications and their implications; clear about scope and limitations
weaknesses: Proof presented as 'Claim' with acknowledged 'proof sketch' rather than complete theorem; key steps incomplete: (i) Gaussian universality for multiple tokens relies on extending [48,41,28] without full details, (ii) replicon condition (Eq. 10) only empirically verified ('AMP converged in experiments'), not analytically proven—this condition is crucial for establishing AMP tightness in non-convex setting yet lacks rigorous validation

Substantial gap between model and practical transformers limits relevance: tied (not separate Q,K,V) attention, single head (not multi-head), Gaussian i.i.d. token inputs (not structured text embeddings), fixed T=O(1) sequences, supervised tasks on synthetic data (not self-supervised pretraining on natural data), identity value matrix

Cannot explain all empirically observed phenomena in real networks: MP target reproduces low-rank structure and outliers but fails to capture power-law tails; authors acknowledge this but defer exploration to future work

Limited technical novelty in proof techniques: predominantly adapts existing frameworks (AMP [38,39,51], Gaussian universality [41,28,48], GMT [49,50], spin-glass methods [33,34,35]); extension to multiple tokens and softmax is useful but incremental

Replicon condition (Eq. 10) not analytically verified; complex expression involving ReLU and second derivatives; relying on post-hoc convergence of AMP algorithm as validation is backwards reasoning and limits confidence in theoretical guarantees

Algorithmic insights limited: characterizes global minima but not optimization dynamics; does not explain why non-convex attention loss is trainable by gradient descent—acknowledged as 'challenging problem for future work'

Finite-dimension behavior not characterized: no analysis of minimal d for asymptotic validity, convergence rates, or finite-d effect scaling; simulations use d=100-200 but asymptotic regime not explicitly confirmed
Main empirical validation uses narrow hyperparameter range (λ=0.01, β=β₀=1, Δ=0.5, T=2); limited systematic exploration of sensitivity across parameter space

strengths: Novel theoretical framework providing first high-dimensional asymptotic analysis linking spectral properties to generalization in attention layers
Rigorous mathematical development combining random matrix theory, spin-glass theory, and approximate message passing in an integrated framework
Comprehensive experimental validation showing excellent agreement between theory and gradient descent across multiple regimes
Interpretable error decomposition (overfitting, underfitting, approximation, mismatch terms) that connects spectral structure to generalization
Qualitative predictions of empirical phenomena in real transformers (low-rank structure, spectral outliers, power-law scaling)
Honest and thorough discussion of model limitations and assumptions
Practical insights about factorized vs non-factorized parameterization and inductive biases of weight decay
Clear presentation with informative figures and extensive reproducible details in appendix
weaknesses: Main results formulated as 'Claims' rather than theorems; complete proofs require substantial additional technical development, and replicon condition verified only numerically
Conjecture E.1 (extension beyond strict scaling regime) is crucial for Section 4 and 5 results but lacks rigorous proof despite strong numerical support
Highly simplified model with restrictive assumptions: tied attention, single head, synthetic attention-indexed tasks, Gaussian data, finite T=O(1)
Large gap between theoretical model and practical transformers; predictions only validated on synthetic data, not real transformers or datasets
Limited mechanistic justification for why factorization outperforms despite reduced expressivity; nuclear norm connection deserves more prominence
Computational cost (60,000 CPU hours) and complexity of state evolution equations may limit reproducibility
Theoretical framework does not address multi-head attention, which is standard in practice
Power-law scaling laws derived for specific target structure; unclear if mechanism applies to realistic data distributions
